title: Choroidal Hemangioma: A Clinical Masterclass

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: A choroidal hemangioma is a benign, vascular hamartoma of the choroid. It occurs in two distinct clinical forms: Circumscribed (CCH), which is typically a sporadic, solitary tumor in adults, and Diffuse (DCH), which is usually associated with Sturge-Weber Syndrome (SWS) and presents in childhood. While histologically benign, these tumors cause significant morbidity via exudative retinal detachment and macular edema.

sections.title: Clinical Features & Presentation
content: Metamorphopsia and micropsia due to subretinal fluid
Progressive hyperopic shift (tumor pushing retina forward)
Circumscribed: Orange-red, dome-shaped mass (mean 3-7mm thick)
Diffuse: Widespread thickening, 'Tomato Catsup' fundus appearance
Overlying RPE changes: Fibrous metaplasia or hyperplasia over time
Secondary Glaucoma (more common in Diffuse/SWS)

sections.title: Pathophysiology & Genetics
sections.content: Composed of large, thin-walled vascular channels (cavernous, capillary, or mixed). Endothelial lining is mature. Recent evidence suggests somatic GNAQ (Arg183) mutations in Sturge-Weber related DCH, similar to Port-wine stains, distinguishing them from GNAQ Q209 mutations found in Uveal Melanoma.

sections.title: Diagnostic Imaging: The 'Washout' Pathognomonic
content: Step 1: FFA - Early lacy filling of large choroidal vessels in the arterial phase.
Step 2: FFA - Intense late staining/pooling in cystic retinal spaces.
Step 3: ICG (Gold Standard) - Rapid, intense hyperfluorescence within seconds.
Step 4: ICG Washout - Late phase (20-30 min) shows 'washout' of dye, leaving the tumor hypofluorescent compared to normal choroid.

rows: High initial spike, high internal spikes

sections.title: Management Strategy for CCH
content: 1. Observation: If asymptomatic and no SRF.
2. Photodynamic Therapy (PDT): Gold standard for symptomatic CCH.
3. Plaque Brachytherapy: For thick tumors (>4mm) unresponsive to PDT.
4. Proton Beam Therapy: High success but increased risk of radiation retinopathy.
5. Anti-VEGF: Adjuvant for refractory edema (limited efficacy alone).

sections.title: PDT Protocol (Standard of Care)
content: Verteporfin Dose: 6 mg/m2 body surface area
Infusion: 10 minutes; Laser at 15 minutes
Laser Parameters: 689 nm, 50 J/cm2 intensity
Exposure Time: 83-100 seconds per spot
Goal: Selective vascular occlusion without RPE damage
Success: >90% SRF resolution in CCH

sections.title: Sturge-Weber Syndrome (DCH) Management
content: Systemic Beta-Blockers (Propranolol): Emerging therapy for DCH in infants
External Beam Radiotherapy (EBRT): 20-30 Gy for diffuse cases
Glaucoma Control: High risk of intraoperative suprachoroidal hemorrhage
Prophylaxis: Scleral thickening/stasis in SWS may require prophylactic sclerotomies during surgery

sections.title: Critical Red Flags
content: Rapid growth (Suspect Melanoma or Metastasis)
Total Exudative RD (Leads to neovascular glaucoma)
Low Internal Reflectivity on B-Scan (Suggests Melanoma)
Lipofuscin pigment on surface (Suggests Melanoma)
Port-wine stain in children (Screen for glaucoma/DCH)

content.explanation: High Internal (Reflectivity), Hemangioma Orange. (A-Scan/B-Scan reflectivity is high; Fundus appearance is orange).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Exam High-Yields
content: Unlike melanoma, choroidal hemangiomas NEVER transform into malignant tumors.
The 'washout' sign on ICG is the most specific test to differentiate from melanoma.
CCH usually occurs at the posterior pole (temporal to disc/macula).
DCH in Sturge-Weber can lead to 'Bupthalmos' due to early-onset glaucoma.
Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) can occur even without subretinal fluid.

sections.title: Landmark Studies & Recent Advances
sections.content: The use of Photodynamic Therapy (PDT) revolutionized CCH treatment, as shown in multiple case series (e.g., Jurklies et al.), demonstrating high rates of tumor regression and fluid resolution with minimal collateral damage compared to historical Xenon arc or Argon laser photocoagulation. Recent studies explore Oral Propranolol for DCH in pediatric SWS patients with promising results in reducing tumor thickness and SRF.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Exudative Retinal Detachment (Most common cause of vision loss)
RPE Atrophy and Fibrosis (Permanent vision loss even if fluid resolves)
Neovascular Glaucoma (NVG) in chronic total RD
Prognosis: Good for tumor control; Variable for vision depending on chronicity of foveal detachment
